Author: @Krom5072
Content:
This is my first dislike on an MKBHD video in, like, ever, motivated by the fact that Marques missed a massive opportunity to research the prosthetics decently and present an honest overview of this technology. (Attention, long read.)

While these new bionic hands may have all these fancy servos that operate each finger individually, the control mechanism is truly ancient. Using these 2 myoelectric sensors to control opening/closing of the hand is a technology invented in the Soviet Union in the 1950s, and it has remained essentially unchanged since then. Finer newer sensors enable partial control (user can flex their muscles partially to close the hand partially) or some function by actuating both sensors simultaneously (which in a 1950s hand would do the equivalent of BSoD), but really that's about it. As mentioned in the video, the control over functions of the fingers is relegated to the app. For most prosthetics that support this, it means that the user has to manually change (pun not intended) what mode the prothetic is on: full hand closure, move index finger, make some gesture, etc. (or, in the better cases, this can be controlled with the double actuation mentioned above), which, as you can imagine, can be non-trivial for someone who's had both hands amputated, if we're talking about a smartphone touchscreen. At any rate, any functionality that is not basic fist opening/closing seems to be a weird party trick, rather than anything useful.
For these reasons, while the fingered hand is the more naturally appealing option for amputees - their live hand had fingers so they want the prosthetic to have fingers too - its functionality is really bad. Marques demonstrates this very well by not being able to complete basic tasks. The problem is, the hand can be closed, but the fingers do not curl into a fist like they do in a live hand (well, they can in expensive models, but your brain can't 'order' them to do it with just 2 basic inputs), so the grip is outright bad. Picking up something like a mug is not difficult but imagine if you dropped a coin or a credit card on the floor, or a fragile cookie on yourself while eating, and you need to pick it up with this bulky device, while a bunch of people around you are looking at you annoyedly and annoyingly. The more functional design (that's still not free of control limitations) is something that resembles like a crab's claw or a clamshell grab, two 'fingers' with a rubber buffer between them that provide a much finer and tighter grip when they close; it's much simpler mechanically too and thus cheaper; yet, this kind of prosthetic is almost never promoted commercially because at the first glance it's just not that appealing.
Not being able to use the full functionality of the fancy servos (and not coming remotely close to the operation of a live hand) is one thing, but maintenance of these prosthetics is another. Because this is such an intricate minituarized piece of technology, it is notoriously expensive and unreliable. The case with the sensors (what goes on arm) is usually sturdy enough but the actual hand easily breaks from basic use (not to mention they are not protected against water damage usually) and repairs are cost-prohibitive at which point the 'power user' of the prosthetic (say someone who's had both hands amputated and thus relies on the bionics heavily) racks up an ongoing cost which is comparable to maintaining a luxury brand car. Some governments cover up the expenses partially but this usually involves the initial purchase of the hand, not replacements/repairs. Remember I told you about the clamshell grabs, do you know which form of prosthetic is way more popular than them, or the fingered bionic hands, among actual amputees? The 19th century mechanical 'hook' design which works on cables that go around the body (basically to operate you have to flex your back and/or shoulders in a certain way) and costs way cheaper than any electrical option, not to mention that many amputees just build their own hooks once they get used to how it works. The operation of the hook may sound weird to you but it ends up way more natural for the body to adapt to, and at all kinds of dexterity competitions for people with prosthetics the hooks blow any bionics out of the water. And yeah the fancier hooks cost 700$ but fancier bionics get into six figures. And you know what's miles more popular than even hooks? Non-functional cosmetic prosthetics (basically rubber toys that look like a hand) which can only hold small objects by means of shoving them between their fingers.
Not to mention various other tiny issues like weight (unlike for a live hand, you DO feel this several-kg object on your arm constantly) or sweating of arms under the case (which can throw off the sensors making the hand uncontrollable).

The problem with this video, as with many other videos on this topic, is the mental harm it can cause to amputees. Nobody 'plans' to lose a hand or two so the general public would not be well-researched on this matter. Videos like this, despite depicting how prosthetics are unintuitive to operate and can need 'getting used to', create for a recent amputee an illusion that a device like this, if only you could afford it or waste months convincing your insurance company (or the government) to buy it for you, will fix your life and will work just like the real hand. No, no it won't. Using a prosthetic IS a massive improvement to the quality of life but it still sucks badly. Here, Marques doesn't praise the prosthetics too much, but he absolutely fails to criticize the slow innovation in this area and predatory marketing practices by prosthetic companies that make an overhyped, barely functional product and make fortunes selling it to desperate people.This I consider to be journalistic malpractice.

Author: @erikmortensen2987
Content:
Point of clarification! As EMG tech will likely become more and more mainstream, it is probably worth understanding how it works, and not spreading incorrect descriptions. you and other reviewers, both for this product and the meta wristband, have described EMG as measuring the nervous activity driving the intended movement. This is completely incorrect. EMG, electromyography, as the name implies measures the voltage changes from depolarization of the underlying muscles, NOT the nerves. This signal is several orders of magnitude larger, compared to that of the nerves, which would require micro electrodes to be inserted directly to be measured. What you describe is possible over the brain (EEG), but only because you would here be measuring millions of synchronised neurons, and even then the signal to noise is pretty terrible
- phd in neuroscience, having worked with both techniques

Author: @michaelkielstra6089
Content:
So:
(1) There's an app.  What's the privacy policy like?  Do they get to collect and sell data about what you do with your hand?
(2) What happens if Psyonic goes out of business and their servers shut down?  Do the hands/apps still work, or does the app need to phone home every time you turn it on?
(3) Is this in any way open source, or are people locked in to using their prosthetics -- parts of their bodies -- only in the ways of which the Psyonic black box approves?
(4) If police are trying to hassle you, can they ask Psyonic to override your hand to keep you from, say, driving a car?
(5) What about future-proofing?  One day, Psyonic will shut down, and they'll stop updating their app, and then newer versions of smartphones, or whatever we have then, won't support it.  Again, is the protocol sufficiently open-source that someone could build an alternative client, or will users have to carry around an ancient phone just for controlling their hand?  What happens to them when that phone breaks and they can't get another one because nobody has manufactured them in ten years?
Prosthetic tech is amazingly cool, but it must must must be fully standalone.  People will be relying on this day in, day out, for years.  It absolutely cannot afford to be built in the usual Silicon Valley manner.

Author: @NoName-ik2du
Content:
Very mixed feelings on this.  Having this covered by health insurance makes this a legitimate tool and not just a novelty, _but_ is it _really_ going to be covered by insurance?  Or will you just get the typical runaround of repeated denials, never actually getting the thing you need?

Insurance aside, having an app immediately takes away almost all legitimacy of this product.  If it can function without the app, then I'm still into it.  But if it requires the app, then it's just destined to become overpriced e-waste like every other app-dependent product.  If the app is required, that means the company who produces it can easily turn it into a subscription-based product, or if they go under (or simply want to force you into buying another one) support for the app or product can be dropped with no warning, leaving you with a fancy hand-shaped brick.

Author: @Blearky
Content:
I saw a reel of this the other day where the hand just crawled across the floor because it has the wireless feature 😆

Two things came to mind:

First, please try playing frisbee with it, if the company allows it, of course. The beauty lies not just in getting the basics right, but also in the extra features, so that everyone with a prosthetic can enjoy life as much as they could with their biological hand.

Second, this one’s more of a utopian idea: imagine something like the Olympics, but for the "hardware". While there's a lot of drama around "unfair advantages," I feel like an event where companies can showcase what their tech is capable of would seriously push the field forward. It could spark new knowledge, attract investor interest, and, most importantly,drive scientific progress and innovation.

Amazing video as always, Marques!

Author: @Lord_zeel
Content:
It needs a better pen grip (maybe it does and you were just testing the wrong grip?). When I grip a pen, there are three points of contact: Thumb, index, and the side of the middle finger. The pen is trapped in the middle of the three, and can't just slide out. This is much different from a pinch grip, which only applies force from two directions allowing the item to twist easily, and slide out the side. It looks to me like all they need to do is move the middle finger down toward the palm in order to achieve this, though since it doesn't look like the fingers have any side-to-side motion, it might not apply enough force. Still, with the right application of thumb pressure I'm sure there's a way to make it hold a pen more securely. 

Anyway, I love seeing tech like this. It's frankly absurd just how far behind a lot of medical and assistive technology is simply because the companies that have traditionally made these things don't innovate, charge far far too much, and use medical device regulations to prevent competition from entering the market. I freaking love seeing all the 3D printed prosthetics that have been coming out in the last few years, and this things is super cool too. I hope more companies and more makers continue to push the envelope and make prosthetics and assistive tech just as good, affordable, and accessible as smartphones and other commodity electronics.

Content:
As a person with one arm I'm always sceptical on these products as I've tried many different prosthetics that are cumbersome and in the end more strenuous on your remaining limb, this look like a good step in the right direction, but as a person who has used these types of prosthetics there's a very big 'lag' between input, action and desired result. I am quite anti-ai personally however this is one of those cases that I could see a great use for AI, maybe an ultra-wide camera built into the hand with context from a visual AI to help almost automate the desired gesture for what the user wants to do would be great.

Obviously I am super appreciative of the teams of people that work to give people like myself a better quality of life. Thank you for a shining a light on this Marques :)

Content:
A remote control app for it and this tube thing used to let people who still have hands wear and use the device and the fact that they look intuitive and clean means they had to spend time designing and developing these things which aren't super useful to people who actually need a prosthetic hand and the fact that the device itself looks cool are just all red flags for me. It's as if Meta, Google, Apple, Tesla or some Silicon Valley tech startup came up with a prosthetic hand. They come from the tech(and money) side of things instead of coming from the medical side of things which is always more flashy and less useful.

I'm not trying to be a downer here and I'm all for humanity continue to push the boundaries of technology for actually helping each other but I just hate it when "the money people" pay "tech people" to make stuff for them that looks like it works and is easy to use and that everyone can use it and the "marketing people" say it's "to help" when what it is is just another way to make more money. Like Apple with their whole "not including a charging brick with their phone" thing and using it as a "save the environment" or "going green" BS. Load of crap.

I just hope my pessimism turns out to be proven completely wrong and that this company actually turns it into an actual prosthetic hand that's attainable by as many people who need it as possible. Humanity has done really poorly the past 10-15 years on a scale of "humanity". We suck.

Author: @wdkrebs
Content: If you’ve lost a limb due to a traumatic injury, there’s good chance you are covered by insurance, workers comp, or VA. For congenital amputees, very few insurance companies cover anything more than a body powered prosthetic; you know, the fiberglass arms with a metal hook. Those missing a leg have a hard time getting anything other than crutches or a basic wheelchair covered. I was a test subject for the Luke Arm project and would benefit from a bionic arm, but insurance won’t cover “CPU prosthetics”, so I go without, as do many of my amputee friends.

Author: @griffinrupe
Content: The way you have to review this is by assuming the company is already out of business. What can this product do in the absence of the company (and app) behind it? If the answer is 'not much', then the product is worth 'not much'. I love this kind of accessibility tech, but when the life cycle of a tech company is like ten to twelve years, you have to take this into account. I wish this had been addressed in the video. Giving credit where it's due, Psyonic does seem to have a GitHub page where they've open-sourced all the code for the Ability Hand. Overall a really high level review for something that probably deserves a deeper look to really assess the quality of the product.

With your natural limb you sense where it is in space without looking at it, you sense what you are touching, you sense how much force you are applying. With that constant feedback you are able to 100% of the time output any changes and movements you want without error and with extreme precision because of those seances.

With a bionic, no matter how intricate it is, the barrier is still your ability to quickly communicate with it and for it to communicate with you.

This is exactly why you see amputees prefer to not wear anything at all and just use their stub or to use a more mechanical, lever and pulley based prosthetic.

Great to see companies innovating and bringing the price down. But understand where the true barriers lie.
